981.title: Udham Singh, 1940
981.hook: a survivor of Jallianwala shot the former Punjab governor in London and was hanged
981.howItsDone: Udham Singh is honored in Punjab as a shaheed; his memorials, his name on public places and his anniversary are kept there, and his story is told alongside the memory of Jallianwala Bagh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, siropa: a robe of honor given to the wrong man, and outrage that became reform. Today, one man who carried Jallianwala Bagh for a very long time.

London, 1940. A meeting hall in Westminster, full of officials and guests listening to speeches about India. Near the end, a man in the audience stands up, draws a revolver and fires. Among those hit is Sir Michael O'Dwyer, who had been lieutenant governor of Punjab when the troops fired at Jallianwala Bagh. O'Dwyer dies. The man with the gun is seized before he can leave the hall. His name is Udham Singh, and he has come a very long way, in miles and in years, to stand in that room.
screen: `A MEETING HALL IN LONDON.` → `A MAN STANDS AND FIRES.` → `HE IS SEIZED IN THE HALL.`

segments.voice: Udham Singh grew up in an orphanage in Amritsar. Sikh and Punjabi memory holds that he was at Jallianwala Bagh on the day of the firing, and that what he saw never left him. Some historians question whether he was there, and the sources don't settle it. Either way, the lieutenant governor who had backed the general became, for him, the name of that day. He didn't act quickly. He traveled, worked, was jailed, and eventually reached England; the shooting came long after the garden. Accounts of his trial say he gave his name as Ram Mohammad Singh Azad: a Hindu name, a Muslim name and a Sikh name together, and azad, which means free. He was tried, convicted and hanged in London. In Punjab he's honored as a shaheed, a martyr, and his ashes were later brought home. Others, then and since, have judged the killing differently, and the Sikh tradition itself teaches deep caution about anger. The name he chose points to something the Guru Granth Sahib says plainly. At Ang 1349, Bhagat Kabir sings that from one light the whole world came into being, so who can be called good and who bad? Whatever people conclude about his act, that name refused to divide the people of Punjab.

982.title: Bhagat Singh
982.hook: born into a Sikh family, the young revolutionary later wrote of doubting God, and is honored across Punjab
982.howItsDone: Bhagat Singh is remembered across Punjab, by Sikhs and by others, as a shaheed of the freedom struggle; his picture hangs in homes and shops, and his anniversary is marked with gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Udham Singh, and a long memory carried from Amritsar to London. Today, a young man whose face is painted on walls across Punjab.

On a truck's back panel, a college wall, a sticker on a scooter: the same young face, a mustache, sometimes a turban, sometimes a hat tilted to one side. Ask the driver who it is and you'll get two words, said with real pride. Bhagat Singh. Ask what he believed about God, and the answer gets more interesting. He was born into a Sikh family. And near the end of his short life, in a prison cell, he wrote out, as carefully as he could, why he no longer believed.
screen: `THE SAME FACE ON TRUCKS AND WALLS.` → `TURBAN OR HAT.` → `A PRISON CELL, AND A PEN.`

segments.voice: Bhagat Singh grew up in a Sikh household in Punjab, in a family already caught up in the struggle against British rule. As a young man he turned to armed struggle, and that path ended in a trial in Lahore. He was hanged there with two companions, Sukhdev and Rajguru. While waiting in prison he wrote a piece titled Why I Am an Atheist. He explains, plainly and without mockery, how he came to doubt God, and insists he got there by thinking it through, not out of pride. He writes, too, that he expects to face the gallows without turning to belief for comfort at the end. He's honored across Punjab and beyond by religious and non-religious people alike. Some Sikhs who pray every morning keep his picture on the wall; those who share his doubt claim him too. Nobody needs to settle his beliefs to honor his courage and his candor. Guru Nanak gives the Sikh measure of a life at Ang 62 of the Guru Granth Sahib: truth is higher than everything, but higher still is truthful living. Bhagat Singh's conclusions about God are his own, and Sikh teaching doesn't share them. What his admirers point to is that he didn't pretend. He said what he thought, and lived it to the end.

983.title: The SGPC, 1920
983.hook: Sikhs formed a committee to manage gurdwaras and a volunteer band, the Akali Dal
983.howItsDone: The SGPC today manages historic gurdwaras in Punjab and neighboring regions, including the Golden Temple; Sikhs also do seva in gurdwaras everywhere as volunteers, in the kitchen, cleaning and looking after shoes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhagat Singh: an honest mind, honored by believers and doubters alike. Today, back to the gurdwaras, where the outrage over the robe turns into a plan.

Four letters on signboards and letterheads in Punjab: S, G, P, C. You can pass them without a second look. Behind them is a long name, the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, and behind the long name is a question Sikhs had been asking since the robe was given to the general. Who should look after the gurdwaras? In 1920, at a gathering in Amritsar, Sikhs gave their answer. We will.
screen: `FOUR LETTERS ON SIGNBOARDS.` → `A LONG NAME BEHIND THEM.` → `WHO LOOKS AFTER THE GURDWARAS?`

segments.voice: Gurdwaras were then often in the hands of mahants, hereditary custodians, and some treated the shrines and their lands as private property. Reformers said practices had crept in that went against the Gurus' teaching, and at the Golden Temple the manager answered to the government. In 1920 Sikhs met in Amritsar and formed a committee to manage the gurdwaras on behalf of the Panth, the whole Sikh community. Its long name means, roughly, the chief committee for managing the gurdwaras. Alongside it came a band of volunteers, the Akali Dal. Akali comes from Akal, the Timeless One, a name for God. The Akalis weren't paid soldiers. They were farmers, teachers, former servicemen and students who gave their time, and later their bodies, to the work. Guru Nanak says at Ang 26 of the Guru Granth Sahib that if you serve in this world, you'll be given a seat in the court of the Lord. The reform movement was political, and the SGPC later became a powerful elected body. But at the start it ran on seva: ordinary people taking on a job no one was paying them for.

984.title: Tarn Taran, 1921
984.hook: reformers were attacked seeking to take over the gurdwara
984.howItsDone: Sikhs visit the gurdwara at Tarn Taran, with its large sarovar, as a historic shrine; the reformers who died there are remembered among the martyrs of the gurdwara reform movement.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the SGPC, and volunteers who stepped up for the gurdwaras. Today they arrive at one, and it goes badly.

Early in 1921, a band of reformers walks into a town south of Amritsar, where a gurdwara stands beside a wide sacred pool; tradition says Guru Arjan founded the town. They've come, singing, to ask the priests who hold the shrine to hand it over to the Panth. They talk, and wait to be heard. Night falls. They're still there, waiting, when the priests' men come at them with weapons.
screen: `A SACRED POOL SOUTH OF AMRITSAR.` → `REFORMERS COME TO TALK.` → `AT NIGHT, AN ATTACK.`

segments.voice: The reformers accused the custodians at Tarn Taran of allowing practices that went against the Gurus' teaching, and of treating the shrine's offerings as their own. They came to take over its management for the newly formed committee. Accounts say that while they waited, the priests and the men with them attacked, striking the reformers with sticks and blades. Several were badly wounded, and some died of their wounds. The reformers didn't answer the attack with an attack. They held their ground and cared for the wounded, and in the end the shrine passed to the Panth's management. Calm, here, didn't mean quiet. It meant not letting someone else's violence choose your next move. In a salok at Ang 1427 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Tegh Bahadur praises the one who frightens no one and fears no one. Both halves matter: they came without frightening anyone, and didn't run when they were frightened. Tradition explains the name Tarn Taran as a boat that carries people across. That night, the people at the pool needed something to carry them through, and they found it in staying still.

985.title: Nankana, the full story
985.hook: at Guru Nanak's birthplace in 1921 the mahant's men killed many peaceful reformers, including Bhai Lachhman Singh
985.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Nankana massacre as the Saka Nankana Sahib, with an annual remembrance in February; pilgrims to Gurdwara Janam Asthan bow at the jand tree associated with Bhai Lachhman Singh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tarn Taran: calm under attack. Today, the same test, at the place tradition holds as Guru Nanak's birthplace.

In the courtyard of a gurdwara at Nankana Sahib stands an old jand tree, a thorny tree of the Punjab plains. Pilgrims stop beside it and bow their heads. It isn't there for its shade. Sikhs remember what was done at that tree on a morning in 1921, at the place tradition holds as Guru Nanak's birthplace. To understand why people bow to a tree, you need the whole story.
screen: `AN OLD JAND TREE IN A COURTYARD.` → `PILGRIMS BOW BESIDE IT.` → `THE WHOLE STORY.`

segments.voice: The gurdwara at Guru Nanak's birthplace was held by a mahant, Narain Das, who ran it as his own. Reformers accused him of misusing its wealth and allowing wrongs within its walls, and meant to bring it under the Panth's care. Accounts say the mahant knew they were coming and gathered armed men. A band of reformers led by Bhai Lachhman Singh reached the gurdwara early in the morning. They went in, sat down before the Guru Granth Sahib, and began to recite. The gates were shut behind them, and the mahant's men opened fire and attacked with blades. Accounts say the reformers had pledged not to resist, and they didn't strike back. Many were killed in the hall and the courtyard. Sikh memory holds that Bhai Lachhman Singh, wounded, was tied to the jand tree and burned. That's why pilgrims bow there. Baba Farid, whose words are in the Guru Granth Sahib at Ang 1378, says that if someone strikes you with their fists, don't strike them in return; kiss their feet and go home. Farid is speaking of the inner life, not of a massacre. But some readers hear his salok beside Nankana, because the reformers lived it at a terrible cost. The news spread across Punjab, and the shrine soon passed into the Panth's care.

986.title: The keys, 1921
986.hook: the Sikhs won back the keys of the Golden Temple treasury by peaceful protest
986.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the keys affair, the Chabian da Morcha, as an early victory of the gurdwara reform movement, won by peaceful protest; the toshakhana of the Golden Temple is still kept under the SGPC's management.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nankana: reformers who did not strike back, at a terrible cost. Today, the same refusal, and this time it wins something.

A bunch of keys on a ring. They open the toshakhana, the treasury of the Golden Temple, where its precious gifts and offerings are kept. In late 1921, just as the new Sikh committee asks for them, an official acting for the British government takes them into the government's hands. On paper it's a small administrative step. To Sikhs, it's a message: you may pray here, but we still hold the keys. What happens next turns a bunch of keys into a national story.
screen: `A BUNCH OF KEYS.` → `THE TEMPLE'S TREASURY.` → `TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT.`

segments.voice: The SGPC had begun to manage the Golden Temple. Taking the treasury keys into government hands said the British, not the Sangat, still had the last word. Sikhs answered with meetings, speeches and refusals, all peaceful. Leaders were arrested, including Baba Kharak Singh, a respected head of the committee. More volunteers stepped forward and were arrested in their turn. The protest spread, and the arrests didn't stop it. In the end the government backed down. The prisoners were released, and the keys were handed to Baba Kharak Singh. Accounts say Mahatma Gandhi sent a telegram of congratulation, calling it the first decisive battle for India's freedom won. In a salok at Ang 1237 of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru is called the key: the mind is a locked room, and only the Guru's key opens it. That verse is about the inner life, not a treasury. But it points at what Sikhs remember about this protest: in their telling, the keys in the government's keeping were never the real power; the Sangat's discipline was. Without striking anyone, the community won back what was theirs, and more battles were coming.

segments.voice: If there's a key nearby, hold it in your palm and feel its weight; if not, picture one. 987.title: Guru ka Bagh, 1922
987.hook: volunteers took police beatings without striking back, and the world saw it
987.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru ka Bagh as one of the peaceful campaigns of the gurdwara reform movement; the gurdwara near Amritsar keeps its memory, and the story is told in histories of the Akali movement.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the keys: a first battle won without a blow. Today ends a week that began with a long memory in London and turned toward the gurdwaras.

Dry branches, an axe, and a kitchen fire that needs feeding. In a village outside Amritsar there's a gurdwara called Guru ka Bagh, the Guru's garden, with land around it where acacia trees grow. Sikh volunteers go out to cut wood for the langar, the free kitchen. The custodian who holds the shrine says the land and the trees are his. The police arrest the woodcutters for theft. And then more volunteers keep coming, walking toward the police lines with their hands at their sides.
screen: `WOOD FOR THE LANGAR FIRE.` → `ARRESTED FOR THEFT.` → `MORE VOLUNTEERS KEEP COMING.`

segments.voice: Like Nankana and Tarn Taran, Guru ka Bagh was in the hands of a mahant, a hereditary custodian, and the reformers said a Guru's shrine belonged to the whole panth. The wood was a small thing. Who owned the garden was not. Jathas, groups of volunteers, set out each day from the Akal Takht in Amritsar, vowed to stay peaceful. At the garden the police met them with heavy sticks and beat them to the ground. Accounts written at the time describe men falling, getting up, and being struck again, without raising a hand. Charles Freer Andrews, an English clergyman, went to see for himself. He wrote that he watched the blows fall on men who did not strike back, and that the sight brought the crucifixion to his mind. His account was printed and read far beyond Punjab, and that's how the world came to see it. In the Asa di Var, at Ang 470 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says sweetness and humility are the essence of every virtue and all goodness. The volunteers walked to the garden humbly, with no weapon and no curse. But humble didn't mean bowed: when they were knocked down, they got up. The week ran from Udham Singh and Bhagat Singh to the SGPC, Tarn Taran, Nankana and the keys, and it ends here.
